README.md.text:
# Crypto Cost Basis Calculator

Free, browser-only tool for anyone who bought, sold or earned crypto at more than
one price. Paste or open a CSV of your own transactions and it matches every sale
to your purchase lots under FIFO, LIFO, HIFO, LOFO or a tax-aware greedy rule,
splits each sale into short-term and long-term rows, compares the methods side by
side with an estimated tax, lists the coins and basis still held, and exports
Form 8949 style rows. Nothing is uploaded.

**Live tool:** https://duncan-haywood.github.io/monorepo-projects/crypto-cost-basis-calculator/

Open `index.html`. No build step, no dependencies. `node --test` runs the suite.

- `calc.mjs` - CSV parsing with exchange-style header aliases, lot matching,
  holding periods, per-wallet books, tax netting and the Form 8949 style export.
- `form8949Totals` in `calc.mjs`: the Part I (short-term) and Part II (long-term) column totals for the report year, shown under the rows, with a count of rows that have no purchase on record.
- Tax-loss harvesting (`parsePrices`, `harvestPlan` in `calc.mjs`): type today's price per coin and it values every open lot, ranks the lots under water by tax saved, and shows how much of the year's estimated tax selling them would remove. Prices are yours; none are fetched; wash-sale rules are not applied.
- Wait-for-long-term (`waitPlan` in `calc.mjs`, shown under the harvesting prices): gains still short-term that turn long-term within 90 days, with the estimated tax saved by waiting and how far the price can fall before selling now would have kept more cash.
- Sell planner (`planSale` in `calc.mjs`, `--sell BTC --price 90000 --qty 0.1` in the CLI): pick a coin, a price you type and either coins or dollars to raise; it picks lots under each of the five methods and shows the extra tax each adds to the year's result (negative when the sale offsets gains), so you can see before selling which lots to sell.
- Lot-identification record (`idRecord` in `calc.mjs`, `--sell BTC --price 90000 --qty 0.1 --id-record HIFO` in the CLI, a panel under the sell planner on the page): writes out which wallet, purchase date, quantity and basis a planned sale is to use under the chosen method, so you can date it and keep it before selling. Specific identification generally depends on choosing units no later than the sale and being able to show it; whether this record is enough is for your tax professional.
- Gift planner (`donationPlan` in `calc.mjs`, `--donate BTC --price 90000 --qty 0.5 [--deduction-rate 0.3]` in the CLI): picks the lots held over a year with the most gain per coin, shows their market value, the gain that is never taxed and the long-term tax avoided against selling them. Short-term lots are skipped (a gift of those is not valued at market). Deduction limits and appraisal rules are yours to check.
- Wallet-to-wallet transfers (`matchLots` in `calc.mjs`): with per-wallet matching on, a `transfer` row with a `to wallet` column moves lots (purchase date and basis intact, chosen by the selected method) so basis follows the coins; over-transfers are warned, not guessed. Without the column, or with matching off, transfers stay ignored.
- `netCapital` / `carryoverChain` in `calc.mjs`: the $3,000 (or $1,500) annual capital-loss deduction and indefinite carryforward, chained year by year from the first sale in the file, with a table on the page and in the CLI. A loss year now lowers later years' estimated tax instead of vanishing.
- `incomeReport` / `toIncomeCsv` in `calc.mjs`: staking, mining and airdrop receipts for the report year by coin (receipts, quantity, first and last date, value when received) on the page, in the CLI and as a CSV (`--income-csv`), so the ordinary-income side of a crypto year is not buried inside the gains.
- `niit` in `calc.mjs` (`--magi`, `--other-nii`, `--filing` in the CLI; three optional boxes on the page): the 3.8% net investment income tax (Form 8960, simplified). Give your other income for the year and filing status and it charges 3.8% on the smaller of net investment income and the amount your income with the crypto result exceeds $200,000 (single or head of household), $250,000 (joint or qualifying surviving spouse) or $125,000 (separate), shows how much of it the crypto result causes, and adds a surtax column to the method comparison so a method that lowers income tax but not the surtax is visible. Staking and mining income is left to you to add as other income or other investment income, because whether it counts depends on your facts.
- Form 8949 boxes (`form8949Box`, `form8949BoxTotals` in `calc.mjs`): an optional `reported` column on sell rows (`basis` = broker reported it on Form 1099-DA with basis, `nobasis` = reported without basis, blank = not reported) sorts each row into digital-asset box G/H/I (short-term) or J/K/L (long-term), adds a Box column to the 8949 CSV and shows totals per box on the page and in the CLI. Without the column nothing changes.
- Swap rows (`type=swap` with `to asset` and `to quantity` columns in `parseTransactions`): a coin-for-coin or DEX swap is one row, booked as a taxable sale of the coin given up and a buy of the coin received, both at the USD `total` you enter for that day (the fee lowers proceeds). Missing second coin or value is an error, never a guess.
- Tax-software import file (`toTurboTaxCsv`, `turboTaxSkipped` in `calc.mjs`, `--tax-software <file>` in the CLI, a button under the sell planner): the year's sales as the five-column crypto template online filing products document (Currency Name, Purchase Date, Cost Basis, Date Sold, Proceeds; MM/DD/YYYY), so a result matched here can be loaded where you file. Sales with no purchase on record are left out and counted, never given a zero basis. Check the column layout against your filing product's current template before importing.
- `importers.mjs` - Coinbase, Kraken, Binance.US, Binance (global spot trade history), Crypto.com App, Gemini, Bitstamp, Cash App account activity, Robinhood account activity (crypto rows only; stocks ignored), Koinly universal CSV and Coinbase Pro fills export readers that produce the plain CSV `calc.mjs` reads (unpriced rows left empty and flagged, never zero).
- Koinly universal CSV reader (`importKoinly` in `importers.mjs`): buys and sales against USD, coin-for-coin swaps split into a sale and a buy at Koinly's USD Net Worth value, labelled staking/mining/airdrop receipts as income; unlabelled transfers, non-USD fiat and non-USD fees are skipped with a note. Lets someone leaving a paid tax service re-run the five-method comparison locally.
- Map your own columns (`suggestMapping`, `applyMapping` in `importers.mjs`): for an export none of the readers recognise (a broker, a wallet app, your own sheet) the page shows a mapper. Pick which column is the date, type, asset, quantity, USD total or price and fee, say what each type value means (buy, sell, income, transfer, leave out), and it rewrites the file as the plain format on your device. Unreadable rows and missing USD values are listed, never zeroed. No exchange layout is assumed.
- `cli.mjs` - the same matching in a terminal, zero dependencies and no network: `node cli.mjs --method HIFO --year 2024 --form8949 8949.csv coinbase.csv kraken.csv` reads one or more exchange exports (or `-` for stdin), prints gains, the five-method comparison and holdings, and writes Form 8949 style rows; `--prices "BTC=65000,ETH=3200"` prints the tax-loss harvesting and wait-for-long-term views from prices you type, `--json` for scripts, `--per-wallet`, `--short-rate`/`--long-rate`, `--carry-short`/`--carry-long`/`--mfs` for loss carryforward. Exit 2 on bad usage, 1 when no transactions could be read.
- Form 1099-DA check (`parse1099da`, `reconcile1099da` in `calc.mjs`, `--reconcile 1099da.csv` in the CLI): give it the per-coin proceeds and basis your broker reported (CSV `asset,proceeds,basis`) and it compares each coin with your own lot matching, flagging proceeds that differ, basis that differs (the usual sign the broker missed purchases made elsewhere) and coins on only one side. Also on the page, under the coin tables: paste the figures and see the same comparison without a terminal. Your proceeds are net of the sale fee, so a small proceeds gap can just be the fee.
- Wash-sale lookalike (`washLookalike` in `calc.mjs`, shown under the Form 8949 totals and in the CLI): crypto is outside the wash-sale rule today, but for each losing sale it finds the same coin bought or received within 30 days either side (not the lots the sale used, each purchase used once) and shows how much loss a stock-style rule would defer, so a harvesting plan survives a rule change. Informational; never applied to the tax figures.
- `usage.mjs` - local-only feature counters with an opt-out.
- `fifo-vs-hifo-crypto-cost-basis.html` - guide with a worked example that the
  test suite recomputes.
- Search guides, each checked by the test suite against the code: `crypto-tax-loss-harvesting-worked-example.html`, `form-8949-crypto-boxes-g-h-i-j-k-l.html` and `import-coinbase-kraken-binance-csv-crypto-taxes.html`.

## What you use today, and what this does differently

- **A spreadsheet:** free and private, but the lot matching, holding-period split and per-method comparison are yours to build and keep correct for every sale.
- **Crypto tax services** (Koinly, CoinTracker, TokenTax and similar): they sync exchanges and wallets and file-ready reports, but they want an account, your full transaction history on their servers, and usually a paid plan for larger histories. This tool reads exports you already have and keeps them in your browser.
- **Your exchange's own tax report:** convenient, but typically one method and one platform. This tool combines several exports and shows FIFO, LIFO, HIFO, LOFO and a tax-aware rule side by side.
- **A tax professional:** the right place to settle which method you may use and how to file. This tool does not decide that.
- **What this adds:** a five-method comparison on your own CSV with estimated tax, tax-loss harvesting from prices you type, Form 8949 style rows, a zero-dependency CLI, no signup and no upload.

**No warranty.** Free and as-is; arithmetic on figures you type, not legal, tax,
financial or investment advice. It does not fetch prices or connect to exchanges,
and does not model DeFi, NFTs, forks, lost coins, gifts, wash-sale style rules,
state tax or loss limits; the net investment income tax is a simplified estimate that runs only when you enter your other income. Which lot-identification
methods you may use depends on your jurisdiction and records. Unverified against a
real tax return: tested on hand-calculated examples and conservation checks.

**Privacy.** Everything runs in your browser; your transactions are never uploaded.
Anonymous feature counts stay in local storage and can be switched off.

MIT licence, see `LICENSE`.

## Host your own copy

Your data stays in your browser either way, but you can serve the page from an address you control. It is a static
site: the server only hands out files and never sees a figure or a file you load.

- **Docker:** `docker compose up -d`, then open <http://localhost:8080> (`Dockerfile` is nginx plus the page's files).
- **Fly.io:** `fly launch --copy-config --no-deploy --dockerfile Dockerfile`, then `fly deploy` (`fly.toml`).
- **Render:** deploy from your fork with `render.yaml` (static site, no paid plan needed).
- Nothing runs on the author's accounts. The Docker image has not been built in the session that added these files,
  so build it once and open the page before relying on it. Tests: `node --test deploy.test.mjs`.

crypto-tax-loss-harvesting-worked-exampl.text:
← Crypto cost basis calculator

Crypto tax-loss harvesting, with a worked example

Tax-loss harvesting means selling coins that are worth less than you paid so the loss offsets gains you have already realized this year. This page walks one invented portfolio through it with the same arithmetic the free calculator runs, so you can check the logic before you trust it with your own numbers.

Open the free calculator

The example

An investor bought 0.5 BTC on 2023-02-01 for $10,000 and sold it on 2024-09-15 for $30,000: a $20,000 long-term gain, taxed at an assumed 15%, so $3,000 of estimated tax. They still hold three positions, all bought in 2024 and all under water. Prices typed in on 2024-12-10: BTC $60,000, ETH $3,000, SOL $150.

LotCost basisValue at typed priceUnrealizedHeldTax saved if sold alone
10 ETH, bought 2024-03-01$40,000$30,000-$10,000short-term$1,500
100 SOL, bought 2024-05-10$20,000$15,000-$5,000short-term$750
0.2 BTC, bought 2024-04-01$14,000$12,000-$2,000short-term$300

Selling all three realizes $17,000 of short-term losses. Short-term losses are netted against long-term gains when there are no short-term gains, so the year's net gain falls from $20,000 to $3,000 and the estimated tax from $3,000 to $450: $2,550 saved. The saving per lot is ranked on its own against the current result; it is a guide to which lots matter most, not a number that adds up exactly once losses start cancelling each other.

What the calculator does with it

  1. You give it your transactions and, for each coin you still hold, a price you typed. It fetches no prices, so it cannot be wrong about them in the background.
  2. It values every open lot, ranks the ones under water by tax saved, and shows how much of the year's estimated tax selling them would remove.
  3. It also lists gains that turn long-term within 90 days, with the tax saved by waiting and how far the price can fall before selling now would have kept more cash.

The wash-sale question

The wash-sale rule disallows a loss if you buy the same asset within 30 days before or after the sale. Today it is written for stocks and securities, and crypto has generally been treated as property outside it, but that can change and tax advisers differ on edge cases. The calculator never applies the rule to your numbers. It does show, for each losing sale, the same coin bought or received within 30 days either side, and how much loss a stock-style rule would have deferred, so you can see whether your plan still works if the rule is extended.

Before you sell

  • Selling and rebuying costs fees and spread; the calculator uses your typed prices and does not model them for the rebuy.
  • If the market moves between today's typed price and the actual fill, the loss moves with it.
  • Capital losses beyond your gains are deductible only up to an annual limit with the remainder carried forward; the calculator chains that year to year if you give it your history.

Common questions

Is crypto subject to the wash-sale rule?

As the rule is written today it applies to stock and securities, and crypto has generally been treated as property outside it. Proposals to extend it have been discussed, so the calculator shows how much loss a stock-style rule would defer without applying it. Ask a tax professional about your situation.

Which losing lots should I sell first?

The ones that remove the most estimated tax. Short-term losses offset short-term gains, which are taxed at higher rates, so they are usually worth more per dollar than long-term losses. The calculator ranks lots under water by the tax each would save against your current result.

Does the calculator fetch prices?

No. You type today's price for each coin, so nothing leaves your browser and no price feed can be wrong without you seeing it.

No warranty. Free and as-is. Not legal, tax, financial, or investment advice. Every person, trade and price on this page is invented. Tax rules, rates and which lot-identification methods you may use depend on your jurisdiction, your records and the date; confirm with a qualified tax professional.

Use the calculator · FIFO vs HIFO · Licence · GitHub Sponsors

fifo-vs-hifo-crypto-cost-basis.html.text:
← Crypto cost basis calculator

FIFO vs HIFO for crypto cost basis, with a worked example

If you bought the same coin at different prices and later sold some of it, your gain depends on which purchase the sale is matched to. The trades are identical; the matching rule is not, and it can move the estimated tax by thousands of dollars. This page walks one small example through each rule.

Open the free calculator

The example

An invented investor, all in one account. They buy 0.5 BTC on 2023-01-10 for $10,000 plus a $10 fee, 0.5 BTC on 2023-06-15 for $15,000 plus $15, and 0.25 BTC on 2024-02-01 for $12,000 plus $12. On 2024-03-05 they receive 2 ETH from staking worth $5,000. In 2024 they sell 0.6 BTC on 2024-09-20 for $36,000 less a $36 fee, and 1 ETH on 2024-11-02 for $3,300 less a $3 fee. We assume a 24% short-term and 15% long-term rate.

MethodShort-term gainLong-term gainTotal gainEstimated tax
FIFO$797$22,951$23,748$3,634
LIFO$3,770$10,469$14,239$2,475
HIFO$3,770$10,469$14,239$2,475
LOFO$797$22,951$23,748$3,634

FIFO sells the two oldest lots: all 0.5 BTC bought in January 2023 (basis $10,010) and 0.1 BTC of the June lot (basis $3,003). Proceeds are $35,964, so the gain is $22,951, all long-term. HIFO sells the coins that cost the most per BTC, the February 2024 lot ($48,048 per BTC) and then part of the June 2023 lot ($30,030 per BTC), so basis rises to $22,522.50 and the gain falls to $13,441.50 across a short-term and a long-term piece. The ETH sale is short-term under every method, with a $797 gain on $2,500 of basis.

Why the holding period complicates "just use HIFO"

Gains on coins held for more than one year are taxed at long-term rates, which are lower; gains on coins held a year or less are taxed as ordinary income. A high-basis lot you bought recently is short-term, so selling it first can cut the gain but raise the rate. The calculator therefore compares estimated tax as well as gain, and offers a tax-aware rule that orders lots by the tax each coin would trigger at the two rates you enter. That rule picks one sale at a time, so it is a heuristic, not a guarantee of the best plan across a whole year.

Checking your own history

  1. Export every purchase, sale and reward from each exchange and wallet into one CSV with date, type, asset, quantity, USD total, fee and wallet.
  2. Enter coin-for-coin swaps as a sale and a buy at their USD value on the day.
  3. Run it. Fix any warning about a sale larger than the lots on record: that is usually a missing purchase or a transfer in from somewhere you did not export.
  4. Compare the methods, then download the Form 8949 style rows for the method that applies to your records.

Nothing is uploaded: the matching runs in your browser, which matters for a file listing everything you have ever bought.

Common questions

Which method gives the smallest gain?

Usually HIFO, because it sells the coins you paid the most for first. But the holding period matters too: selling a higher-basis coin you have held under a year can cost more tax than selling a lower-basis coin held over a year, because short-term gains are taxed at ordinary rates. That is why the calculator compares tax, not just gain.

Is FIFO the default?

In the United States, property sold without identifying specific units is generally treated as first in, first out. Using HIFO or another method generally relies on identifying the units at the time of sale and keeping records that prove it. Ask a tax professional what applies to you.

Why do exchange reports and my own records disagree?

Exchanges often compute basis only from what happened on their own platform. Coins moved in from elsewhere arrive with no basis, and coins moved out take their history with them. Entering every purchase in one CSV, tagged by wallet, is how you find the gaps; the calculator flags any sale larger than the lots on record.

No warranty. Free and as-is. Not legal, tax, financial, or investment advice. The investor, trades and prices are invented. Tax rules, rates and which lot-identification methods you may use depend on your jurisdiction, your records and the date; confirm with a qualified tax professional.

Use the calculator · Licence · GitHub Sponsors

form-8949-crypto-boxes-g-h-i-j-k-l.html.text:
← Crypto cost basis calculator

Form 8949 boxes G to L for crypto: which box is each sale?

On the 2025 forms, sales of digital assets are reported in their own boxes on Form 8949, separate from stock. Which box a row goes in depends on two facts: how long you held the coins, and whether a broker reported the sale to the IRS on Form 1099-DA, with or without your basis. This page lays out the six boxes and shows how the free calculator assigns each row.

Open the free calculator

The six boxes

HeldBoxWhat the broker reported
One year or less (short-term)GForm 1099-DA, basis reported to the IRS
One year or less (short-term)HForm 1099-DA, basis not reported
One year or less (short-term)INo Form 1099-DA
More than one year (long-term)JForm 1099-DA, basis reported to the IRS
More than one year (long-term)KForm 1099-DA, basis not reported
More than one year (long-term)LNo Form 1099-DA

Short-term rows go in Part I and long-term rows in Part II; the totals carry to Schedule D. Check the current instructions for the form year you are filing, because box lettering and 1099-DA phase-in dates are set by the IRS and can differ from year to year.

How the calculator assigns a box

Add an optional reported column to your sell rows: basis if the exchange reported the sale with basis, nobasis if it reported the sale without basis, and leave it blank if it did not report it. Each row is then sorted into G, H or I when short-term and J, K or L when long-term, a Box column is added to the Form 8949 style CSV it exports, and totals are shown per box. Without the column nothing changes: every row is treated as not reported.

reportedHeld one year or lessHeld more than one year
basisGJ
nobasisHK
blankIL

Why a sale can land in a different box than you expect

  • A sale matched to several lots can be split between a short-term and a long-term row, and the two rows go to different boxes.
  • Changing the matching method (FIFO, HIFO and so on) changes which lots a sale uses, and with it the holding period and the box.
  • Coins moved in from another wallet keep their original purchase date only if the transfer is recorded; otherwise the sale shows up with no basis on record, and the calculator flags it.

Common questions

What is Form 1099-DA?

It is the information return that brokers file for digital-asset sales, starting with transactions in 2025 for gross proceeds and a later year for cost basis, under the IRS schedule. Whether you receive one depends on the platform you used and the year; confirm the current schedule with the IRS instructions.

Do I use box I and L if I got no 1099-DA?

Those are the boxes for digital-asset sales that were not reported to you on a Form 1099-DA, short-term and long-term respectively. The calculator puts a row there when its reported column is blank.

Does the calculator file my return?

No. It produces Form 8949 style rows and totals from your own CSV so you or your preparer can check them against what you file. Nothing is uploaded.

No warranty. Free and as-is. Not legal, tax, financial, or investment advice. Every person, trade and price on this page is invented. Tax rules, rates and which lot-identification methods you may use depend on your jurisdiction, your records and the date; confirm with a qualified tax professional.

Use the calculator · FIFO vs HIFO · Licence · GitHub Sponsors

import-coinbase-kraken-binance-csv-crypt.text:
← Crypto cost basis calculator

Import Coinbase, Kraken, Binance and other exchange CSVs for crypto taxes

Most exchanges let you download your history as a CSV. The free calculator reads those files directly in your browser, converts them to one plain format, and runs FIFO, LIFO, HIFO, LOFO and a tax-aware rule across all of them together, so a coin bought on one exchange and sold on another is matched correctly. Nothing is uploaded.

Open the free calculator

Exports it recognises

  • Coinbase transaction history
  • Coinbase Pro / Advanced Trade fills
  • Kraken ledger
  • Binance.US transaction history
  • Binance spot trade history
  • Crypto.com App transaction history
  • Gemini transaction history
  • Bitstamp transaction export
  • Cash App account activity
  • Robinhood account activity (crypto rows only; stock rows are ignored)
  • Koinly universal CSV

The page detects the format from the column headers. Several files can be loaded at once, or use the command-line version: node cli.mjs --method HIFO --year 2024 --form8949 8949.csv coinbase.csv kraken.csv.

What it will not guess

A coin-for-coin swap, a staking reward or an airdrop often has no dollar value in the export. The importer leaves the total empty and lists the row so you can fill it in from that day's price. It never writes a silent zero, because a zero would overstate your gain on the next sale. Fees paid in a coin rather than dollars are likewise left at zero with a note when the export carries no dollar value for them.

These readers were written from the column layouts the exchanges publish and have not been checked against every real account, so open the result, compare one or two rows with your exchange, and read the notes the importer prints.

If your export is not on the list

The page offers a column mapper: pick which column is the date, type, asset, quantity, USD total or price and fee, say what each type value means (buy, sell, income, transfer or leave out), and it rewrites the file in the plain format on your device. Rows it cannot read, or that have no dollar value, are listed instead of being zeroed.

Leaving a paid tax service

If you have a Koinly universal CSV, the calculator reads buys and sales against USD, splits coin-for-coin swaps into a sale and a buy at Koinly's USD value, and treats labelled staking, mining and airdrop receipts as income. Unlabelled transfers, non-USD fiat and non-USD fees are skipped with a note. It lets you re-run the five-method comparison locally, without an account.

Common questions

Is my transaction history uploaded?

No. The files are read and matched in your browser and are not sent anywhere. Anonymous feature counts stay in local storage and can be switched off.

Why does a row have an empty total?

Because the export did not carry a dollar value for it, for example a coin-for-coin swap or a staking reward. Fill it in from that day's price; the importer leaves it empty on purpose rather than writing zero.

Can I combine several exchanges?

Yes. Load every export, optionally turn on per-wallet matching, and record transfers between wallets with a to-wallet column so basis follows the coins.

No warranty. Free and as-is. Not legal, tax, financial, or investment advice. Every person, trade and price on this page is invented. Tax rules, rates and which lot-identification methods you may use depend on your jurisdiction, your records and the date; confirm with a qualified tax professional.

index.html.text:
CRYPTO COST BASIS CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Which lots did you really sell?

Paste your crypto buys, sales and income as a CSV. The calculator matches every sale to your purchase lots under FIFO, LIFO, HIFO, LOFO or a tax-aware rule, splits each sale into short-term and long-term rows, shows what each method would do to your gain and estimated tax side by side, and exports Form 8949 style rows. Your history stays on your device.

Arithmetic on figures you supply. Not legal, tax, or financial advice. New to this? Read FIFO vs HIFO for crypto, with a worked example. More: tax-loss harvesting, Form 8949 boxes G to L, importing exchange CSVs.

Your transactions

Exchange files are converted to the plain format below and shown in the box, so you can fix or fill in any row before matching. Rows the export gives no USD value for (staking rewards, coin-for-coin swaps on Kraken) are left empty and flagged for you to price.

Type is buy, sell, income (staking, mining, airdrops: basis is the USD value you enter) or transfer (not a sale: ignored unless per-wallet matching is on and the row has a to wallet column, in which case the lots move to that wallet keeping their purchase date and basis; the chosen method decides which lots travel). A coin-for-coin swap is one swap row with to asset and to quantity columns (or two rows: a sale and a buy); it is booked as a sale of what you gave up and a buy of what you got, both at the USD total you give for that day. total is the USD value of the coins before the fee; the fee raises basis on a buy and lowers proceeds on a sale. Use price instead of total if that is what your export has.

Options

Fill in "other income" to add the 3.8% net investment income tax: wages plus any staking or mining income, not counting the results below. It applies only when your income with these results passes $200,000 (single or head of household), $250,000 (joint) or $125,000 (separate). Nothing is estimated while it is blank.

Paste or open your transactions, then click Match my lots.

Map your columns

This file is not one of the exchange layouts the page reads. Say which column is which and what each type value means; it is rewritten as the plain format below on this device. Rows you do not map are left out, and a missing USD value is left empty, never zero.

Result

The same year under each method

MethodShort-term gainLong-term gainTotal gainEstimated tax3.8% surtax

Estimated tax nets short against long results and applies the two rates you entered. It ignores state tax and your other income; the loss-limit table below applies the annual deduction limit and carryforwards. It is a comparison between methods, not a tax bill.

Loss limit and carryforward

YearLoss carried inShort-term gainLong-term gainNet after carry-inDeductible against other incomeCarried to next yearEstimated tax

Years run in order from the earliest sale in your file, so a loss in an early year reduces later gains. Enter any loss you carried in from before the file starts. Net losses deduct up to the annual limit and the rest carries forward with its short or long character. The deduction is shown, not valued, and the table ignores state tax and your other income. Check it against your own Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet.

Form 8949 style rows

DescriptionAcquiredSoldProceedsBasisGain / lossTerm

Totals for Form 8949 and Schedule D

PartRowsProceedsBasisGain / loss

These are the column totals of the rows above: short-term for Part I, long-term for Part II. For 2025 returns the digital-asset boxes on Form 8949 (G to L) depend on whether your broker reported the sale on a Form 1099-DA, so split the rows by box yourself or with your preparer before carrying a total to Schedule D, or add a reported column (basis, nobasis or blank) to your CSV and the totals appear by box.

Income received (staking, mining, airdrops)

AssetReceiptsQuantityFirstLastValue when received

Rows typed as income for the same year as the sales, valued at the USD amount you entered. In the United States this is generally ordinary income when you gain control of the coins, reported apart from capital gains, and the same amount becomes the basis of those coins. The value is yours to document; this is not tax advice.

Coins still held

AssetQuantityRemaining basis

Tax-loss harvesting: what selling your losing lots today would do

Type today's price for each coin you hold (you supply every price; nothing is fetched). The tool values each lot you still hold, finds the ones under water, and shows how much of this year's estimated tax selling them would remove.

Form 1099-DA check: does your broker's form match your own lots?

Brokers now send Form 1099-DA with proceeds, and basis only for coins they saw you buy. Paste the per-coin figures from your form (header asset,proceeds,basis; basis may be blank) and each coin is compared with the lot matching above for the same year. A basis gap usually means the broker did not see purchases made elsewhere; a small proceeds gap can be the sale fee, which your proceeds net out. Nothing leaves this page.

Sell planner: which lots to sell for the least extra tax

Tell it the coin, today's price and either how many coins or how many dollars you want to raise. It sells lots of the coins you still hold under each of the five methods and shows the extra tax each choice adds to the year's result above. You supply the price; nothing is fetched.

How it is calculated

Lots: every buy is a lot with a quantity and a basis (USD total plus fee); every income row is a lot whose basis is the USD value you entered. Matching: sales are processed in date order, with same-day buys available to a same-day sale. Each sale consumes lots in the order the method dictates and is split into one row per lot used, with proceeds (USD total minus fee) and basis shared out by quantity. FIFO sorts by acquisition date, LIFO reverses it, HIFO and LOFO sort by cost per coin, and the tax-aware rule sorts by the tax each coin would trigger at the rates you entered, with the holding period of each lot deciding which rate applies. That rule is a greedy choice made one sale at a time: it is not guaranteed to be the best possible plan across every sale. Holding period: long-term only when the sale date is after the first anniversary of acquisition. Rounding: each row's proceeds and basis are rounded to cents and the gain is their difference, so the rows add up the way a form does.

Not modelled: prices (you supply every USD value), exchange or blockchain imports, DeFi, NFTs, hard forks, lost or stolen coins, gifts, wash-sale style rules, state tax and the effect of the loss deduction on your other tax; the 3.8% net investment income tax is estimated only if you enter your other income and is a simplified Form 8960. A sale larger than the lots on record is shown with zero basis and a warning rather than hidden. Unverified: tested on hand-calculated examples and invariant checks, not on a real return.

Common questions

What is crypto cost basis and why does it matter?

Cost basis is what you paid for a coin, including fees. When you sell, swap or spend it, your taxable gain or loss is the proceeds minus the basis of the specific coins you disposed of. If you bought the same coin at several prices, which purchase counts as the one you sold changes the gain, and the choice of method is the lever you control.

What is the difference between FIFO, LIFO and HIFO?

They are rules for deciding which purchase lots a sale uses up. FIFO sells your oldest coins first, LIFO your newest, and HIFO the coins you paid the most for, which usually produces the smallest gain today. LOFO takes the cheapest coins first. This tool runs all of them on your own history and shows the gain and an estimated tax side by side, so you can see what each choice would have done.

Can I choose any method I like?

Not necessarily. In the United States the default for property is first in, first out, and using another method generally depends on being able to identify the specific units you sold at the time of the sale and keeping records that show it. Whether a method is available to you, and how to document it, is a question for a tax professional; this tool computes what each method would produce, it does not decide what you are allowed to file.

Is my transaction history uploaded anywhere?

No. The matching runs in your browser from the CSV you paste or open from your own disk. Nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts, and it works offline after the page loads. That is the reason to use it for a file that lists everything you have ever bought.

Can I open my Coinbase, Kraken, Binance.US, Crypto.com, Gemini, Bitstamp or Robinhood export directly?

Yes. Open a Coinbase transaction history, a Kraken ledger, a Binance.US, Binance spot trade history, Crypto.com App, Gemini or Bitstamp transaction history, a Cash App account-activity export, a Robinhood account activity report (crypto rows only), a Koinly universal CSV (the export many paid tax tools accept), or a Coinbase Pro / Advanced Trade fills report (or several at once) and the page converts it in your browser into the plain format below, buys and sales paired up, Coinbase Convert rows split into a sale and a buy, and transfers left out. Anything the export gives no dollar value for, such as staking rewards or a Kraken coin-for-coin swap, is left empty and flagged so you can price it from that day's rate; it is never counted as zero. The readers follow the published column layouts and have not been checked against every account type, so skim the converted rows before you rely on them.

What columns does the CSV need?

A header row with date, type, asset, quantity and either a USD total or a price per coin. Fee and wallet are optional. Type is buy, sell, income, swap or transfer. Common exchange headers such as Timestamp, Transaction Type, Quantity Transacted, Subtotal and Fees are recognised. Enter a coin-for-coin swap as one swap row (asset and quantity given up, to asset and to quantity received, total = USD value that day), or as a sale and a buy.

How is the holding period decided?

A gain is long-term when the coins were held for more than one year, meaning the sale date falls after the first anniversary of the acquisition date; a sale on the anniversary itself is still short-term. Each piece of a sale carries the date of the lot it came from, so one sale can produce both short-term and long-term rows.

What does per-wallet matching do?

When it is on, a sale only uses lots recorded in the same wallet or account column, instead of one pool across everything you hold. Some tax rules now expect basis to be tracked wallet by wallet. Turn it on if your records tag each row with where the coins sat, and check the current IRS guidance for how to treat coins you moved between wallets. Add a transfer row with a to wallet column and the lots you move keep their original purchase date and basis in the new wallet, so a later sale there is not shown with zero basis. Network fees paid in coins are not treated as sales.

Does this replace crypto tax software or a tax preparer?

No. It is a private calculator for the matching step on a clean list of rows. It does not connect to exchanges or chains, does not fetch prices, does not understand DeFi, NFTs, forks or lost coins, and ignores wash-sale-style rules, state taxes and the effect of the loss deduction on your other tax; the 3.8% net investment income tax is estimated only if you enter your other income. Use the Form 8949 style CSV as a starting point for your own return or hand it to a preparer.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice and does not replace a tax professional or the instructions to your tax forms. Results are arithmetic on the figures you type; tax rules, rates and reporting requirements change. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before you file anything.

Independent. Not affiliated with any exchange, wallet, blockchain, tax authority or crypto tax software, and none is named or ranked here. The example transactions are invented.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere.

Everything runs in your browser. Your transactions are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (analysis_run, example_loaded, file_opened, report_downloaded) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your data, and are switched off by Do Not Track.

Related tools: for UK rules (Section 104 pool, same-day and 30-day matching) use the UK crypto CGT calculator; the tax-loss harvesting calculator for netting gains and losses before year end, the gambling loss deduction calculator, the quarterly estimated tax calendar and the estimated tax penalty calculator.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.
